messages.author: 594443bd854b12e1
messages.subject: R2WinBUGS license
parts:
I was going to have a look at some R2WinBUGS code for use in
mcmcplots, but I wonder if there's a license issue. R2WinBUGS is under
GPL v2 only, while mcmcplots is GPL v2 or later. My naive
understanding is that if code leaks from R2WinBUGS into mcmcplots,
that effectively means that mcmcplots would be distributing that code
under a more liberal license and infringing the copyrights of the
R2WinBUGS authors.

So that means either the copyright holders (authors) of R2WinBUGS
would need to relicense R2WinBUGS as GPL v2 or later, or changes to
mcmcplots would need to be written from scratch. The latter is
probably easier.

Best,
Ilya

-- Ilya Goldin <www.pitt.edu/~goldin>

My understanding is that the "leaks" in question are

Except that there is no linking of R code to R code in the traditional compiled code sense that Stan links to Eigen and Boost. I believe the CRAN people asked the FSF for a legal opinion and the FSF said that R packages are not considered derivative works of R, despite the fact that R is necessary for R packages. Similarly, one R package can call functions in another R package without being considered a derivative work. But verbatim copying of big chunks of R2WinBUGS code could be an issue for any GPL v2 or later R package.

> that effectively means that mcmcplots would be distributing that code
> under a more liberal license and infringing the copyrights of the
> R2WinBUGS authors.
>
> So that means either the copyright holders (authors) of R2WinBUGS
> would need to relicense R2WinBUGS as GPL v2 or later, or changes to
> mcmcplots would need to be written from scratch. The latter is
> probably easier.
We can ask the R2WinBUGS folks.  Andrew was the original
author, but he's since ceded control.

Ceded maintainership. I keep saying that R2WinBUGS, arm, mi, etc. are in extremely gray areas on questions such as these because insufficient attention was paid to licensing questions and copyright ownership when these R packages were first created. So, I would unfortunately agree that it is probably easier for mcmcplots to either call R2WinBUGS functions or write from scratch.

I've never understood these "GPL vX or later" things.
Why would anyone agree to license their software under
a license that doesn't exist yet?  Or am I misreading
the scope of "or later"?  That's putting a
lot of faith in the license designers.

Your understanding is my understanding, but I am much more pro-GPL (actually I like Affero GPL best) for projects that I do by myself. For me personally, patent issues are a much bigger threat than copyright issues, and software-as-a-service issues are going to bigger than copyright issues in the near future. So, I like that GPL v3 is explicit on patents and Affero is explicit on SAAS, whereas BSD-style licenses say nothing on these fronts.

Ben

I agree that patents are even more innovation-stifling
than GPL. Having been involved in many software-patent
situations (writing, reviewing, finding previous art
to defeat, etc.), all I can say is that I've NEVER seen a software
patent that I thought was worth granting. Every single one
I've ever looked at is trivial (e.g., very general claims,
like connecting a speech recognizer to a DB, stepping down
to claims nobody cares about, like which DB and settings you
use.)

As far as I understand these things, the motivation of
the GPL (and even more the AGPL) is to prevent freeloading
users who take your software and write something closed-source
around it. The copyleft makes them contribute back to the
community. AGPL just extends GPL to software servers, right?

Are there situations where the (A)GPL lets you do more
than BSD?

As an academic, I just want as many people as possible to
use my code, so I prefer BSD.

We went with something like AGPL in our company's open-source
license. That was to explicitly stop companies using the
code without paying us. Companies pretty much all treat
GPL software libraries as poisonous (though they're happy to
use systems like MySQL and Linux). Many of them treat any
open-source as poisonous because of copyright and patent
infringement issues (we've been advised that having our code
as open as it is opens the way to patent and copyright
litigtation that wouldn't be so easy if not everyone could
look at our code).

- Bob

IANAL, nor have I ever been involved in a legal dispute over software, but I think that is basically right. AGPL adds 1 clause to the GPL 3 that roughly says if a server uses modified AGPL code to provide a service, it is distributing a derived work. That is why I think AGPL > GPL, but whether *GPL > BSD is a different debate.

And I think it is fair to say that a primary original motivation for *GPL licenses was to prevent people from distributing derived works without contributing the code back. That is still a big motivation, but nowdays there are other important considerations like patents, signing keys, etc. that are addressed by the FSF's licenses.

As an academic, I just want as many people as possible to
use my code, so I prefer BSD.

I'm in the same boat. But everything depends on what "use" means in practice. To me, if a license says, "you are free to use / modify / etc. this software but whoever might hold the tenuous patents is free to sue your ass for triple damages due to deliberate infringement", then the software isn't really free to use / modify / etc.

I think (and I think the FSF thinks) that GPL3 code developed under federal grants is largely immune from the worst patent-related scenarios. My argument is

1) The Bayl-Dole Act ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayh%E2%80%93Dole_Act ) requires the feds to be given a royalty-free license
2) Section 11 of the GPL3 precludes discriminatory patent deals
3) Thus, everybody is entitled to the same royalty-free patent deal that was given to the feds

But as far as I know, that hasn't been tested in a US court yet. If correct, then there is a tradeoff in that (A)GPL makes it harder for patent trolls but BSD makes it easier for real companies to use the code.

We went with something like AGPL in our company's open-source
license.  That was to explicitly stop companies using the
code without paying us.  Companies pretty much all treat
GPL software libraries as poisonous (though they're happy to
use systems like MySQL and Linux).  Many of them treat any
open-source as poisonous because of copyright and patent
infringement issues (we've been advised that having our code
as open as it is opens the way to patent and copyright
litigtation that wouldn't be so easy if not everyone could
look at our code).

Alas, that is probably true.

Ben

you and me -- we don't (well, maybe I should only speak for myself)

I agree. But if you read patents, people have patents on
things like statistical sampling. How can you avoid the risk?

I believe patents can be announced after you've already built code
that violates them. I believe that's part of the usual patent troll
arsenal of tricks. Suppose two inventors, A and B, generate the same
idea at the same time. Both keep it to themselves, and both build
products based on the idea. If A patents it and B hasn't published
the idea publicly, then A can sue B, even though B generated the
idea completely independently. I think there might be some recourse
for B if they kept detailed records of their own invention -- I know
Bell Labs was fanatical (in theory -- in practice it was chaos) about
keeping hardback dated lab notebooks. Some researchers even had the
habit of having other people sign their lab notebooks for corroboration
as to when they had the idea.

- Bob
